summary: This document specifies using DTLS as a transport for STUN. It gives guidance on when and how to use DTLS with existing STUN usages, and changes the STUN and TURN URIs and the TURN resolution mechanism so they work with DTLS.

eli5.summary: STUN helps devices find out how they look from outside their home network. This RFC lets them ask that question inside a secure, scrambled connection so eavesdroppers cannot listen in.

questions: what port does stun over dtls use
subtitle: Adds DTLS over UDP as a secure transport for STUN and TURN, avoiding the delays of TLS over TCP for real-time media.

tldr.problem: STUN defined TLS over TCP as its secure transport, but TCP is not an optimal transport for the multimedia sessions STUN was meant to support.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7350 adds DTLS over UDP as a valid STUN and TURN transport, reusing the UDP retransmission rules and TLS identity checks. It sets cipher suite requirements, port 5349, the 'stuns' and 'turns' names and a new S-NAPTR tag, 'turn.dtls'.
tldr.outcome: STUN and TURN can be secured over UDP with the same security properties as TLS over TCP. The RFC also says which existing STUN usages gain real benefit from DTLS and which gain little.

today: RFC 7350 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2014. It updates RFC 5389 and RFC 5928, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why STUN Needs DTLS
sections.content:
RFC 5389 defines Transport Layer Security (TLS) over TCP as the secure transport for STUN. But TCP, and so TLS over TCP, is not an optimal transport when STUN is used for its originally intended purpose, which is to support multimedia sessions. The RFC calls this a well documented limitation for real-time communications.

DTLS over UDP offers the same security advantages as TLS over TCP, without those drawbacks. RFC 6347 defines DTLS.
sections.eli5: A careful, check-everything connection can be too slow for a live video call. DTLS gives the same secrecy in a faster style.

sections.title: DTLS as a STUN Transport
sections.content:
STUN already defines three transports: UDP, TCP and TLS. This RFC adds DTLS as a fourth. STUN over DTLS MUST use the same retransmission rules as STUN over UDP and the same server identity checks as STUN over TLS. The rules for keeping connections open and closing them also carry over to DTLS associations.

For cipher suites, implementations MUST support TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, and MAY support others. Perfect Forward Secrecy suites MUST be preferred. Suites with known weaknesses, such as those based on single DES and RC4, MUST NOT be used, and TLS-level compression MUST be disabled.

If the path MTU is unknown, the STUN message must be adjusted for the 13-byte DTLS Record header, the MAC size and the padding size. Classic STUN from RFC 3489 allowed only UDP, so DTLS MUST NOT be used with it, and a request or indication without the magic cookie over DTLS MUST result in an error.
sections.eli5: The rules say which secret-code methods are allowed, which weak ones are banned, and that old-style STUN may not use this. Everything else works like the plain fast version.

sections.title: Port and Service Names
sections.content:
By default STUN over DTLS MUST use port 5349, the same port as STUN over TLS. SRV records can point to a different port. When SRV records are used, the service name MUST be stuns and the protocol name udp.

TURN over DTLS also defaults to port 5349, with the SRV service name turns and protocol name udp. In URIs, secure transports, now including DTLS, MUST use the stuns or turns scheme. For a TURN URI that designates DTLS, the transport value, if set, MUST be udp. A URI that holds an IP address MUST be rejected, unless the domain name comes from the same mechanism that supplied the URI and can be passed to the verification code.
sections.eli5: DTLS uses the same numbered door as secure STUN, door 5349, and its secure web-address starts with the same special words as before.

sections.title: Effect on Each STUN Usage
sections.content:
New STUN usages MUST consider DTLS and say whether the denial-of-service countermeasure from Section 4.2.1 of RFC 6347 is mandatory. The RFC then reviews the existing usages.

  • NAT Discovery: DTLS gives limited benefit, but it stops an active attacker injecting XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS and protects the SOFTWARE attribute. A server MUST implement the countermeasure.
  • Connectivity Check: DTLS would hide some attributes, but MESSAGE-INTEGRITY already protects responses. It would add round trips that delay ICE.
  • Media Keep-Alive: a separate DTLS session would add overhead with minimal security benefit.
  • SIP Keep-Alive: it runs inside a SIP flow, which is protected if SIP over DTLS is used.
  • NAT Behavior Discovery: an Experimental usage, said never to have been effectively deployed. Servers using DTLS MUST implement the countermeasure.
  • TURN: DTLS/UDP is added as a valid transport/allocation combination, and servers MUST implement the countermeasure. TCP allocations MUST NOT be obtained over a DTLS association.
sections.eli5: Not every STUN job gains much from the secret connection. For some it helps a bit, for some it would just slow things down, and for relays it is a good fit.

sections.title: Finding a TURN Server over DTLS
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new S-NAPTR application protocol tag, turn.dtls. It also changes the TURN resolution mechanism of RFC 5928 so DTLS can be found by DNS.

  • The acceptable transport names and the ordered transport list gain 'dtls' and DTLS.
  • If <secure> is true and the transport is 'udp' but the application does not support DTLS, resolution MUST stop with an error.
  • If <secure> is true and no transport is given, but the application supports neither TLS nor DTLS, resolution MUST stop with an error.
  • The default port for DTLS is 5349, and 'turn.dtls' is used when the TURN transport is DTLS.

Using this mechanism does not imply extra DNS round trips; a TURN client starts immediately if the URI contains an IP address.
sections.eli5: To find a relay that speaks the secure style, the phone book lookup gets a new label. If your app cannot speak that style, the lookup stops instead of guessing.

sections.title: Security and IANA Actions
sections.content:
STUN over DTLS adds no security considerations beyond those for STUN over TLS in RFC 5389, and TURN over DTLS adds none beyond those for TURN over TLS in RFC 5766. Using 'udp' as a transport parameter in the 'stuns' and 'turns' URI schemes adds none beyond RFC 7064 and RFC 7065. The new S-NAPTR tag adds none beyond RFC 5928.

IANA registered the turn.dtls tag. It also changed the 'stuns' and 'turns' entries for port 5349 over UDP from 'Reserved for a future enhancement' to 'STUN over DTLS' and 'TURN over DTLS', referencing RFC 7350.
sections.eli5: Because DTLS is just the fast cousin of the older secure method, it brings no new dangers. The official lists were updated to show the new uses.

sections.title: Worked Resolution Example
sections.content: The appendix takes the URI turns:example.net?transport=udp, which gives <secure> true and a DTLS transport. With DNS NAPTR and SRV records and an ordered TURN transport list of DTLS, TLS, TCP and UDP, resolving turns:example.net gives two results in order: DTLS at 192.0.2.1 port 5349, then TLS at 192.0.2.1 port 5349.
sections.eli5: The example shows a lookup that finds the same machine twice: first reached the fast secure way, then the older secure way as a backup.
